allOf.description: Inherits shared step-base properties ($schema, id, owner, created_at, canonical_refs_used).

nfrs.description: Array of non-functional requirements specifying measurable quality attributes for the system. Coverage rule: include at least one NFR for each quality dimension that is explicitly committed to in the charter success_metrics or stakeholder needs. Priority coverage: latency (for any user-facing API), availability (for any service with an SLA), security (for any auth path or PII handling), and durability (for any persistent data). Complete worked example of a single well-formed NFR entry: {"nfr_id": "nfr-auth-p95-latency", "name": "Auth API P95 Latency", "category": "latency", "metric": "P95 response time for POST /auth/login", "target": "< 200ms", "unit": "ms", "measurement_method": "P95 latency from DataDog APM — auth.request.duration metric, averaged over 5-minute windows", "stage": "production", "owner": "api", "trace": [{"type": "derives_from", "id": "metric-auth-p95-latency", "note": "Charter success metric directly motivating this NFR"}]}. Further examples: a checkout API with a latency success metric needs an nfr-latency-checkout-p95 entry; a 24/7 SaaS service needs an nfr-availability-api-uptime entry; a system handling user credentials needs an nfr-security-auth-encryption entry. Anti-patterns: copying NFRs verbatim from a template without grounding them in charter goals (produces unverifiable entries); omitting availability NFRs for a system whose charter commits to 24/7 uptime (breaks traceability-check).

items.description: A single non-functional requirement covering exactly one measurable quality attribute for one component or service. Worked example — a complete entry: {"nfr_id": "nfr-api-auth-p95-latency", "category": "latency", "metric": "P95 response time", "target": "< 200ms", "unit": "ms", "stage": "prod", "owner": "api", "trace": [{"type": "derives_from", "id": "metric-checkout-latency", "note": "NFR enforces the latency target from this success metric"}]}. Create one NFR per quality dimension per component — a single service may have separate NFRs for latency, availability, and throughput because each has a different target, measurement method, and owner. Example: the authentication service warrants nfr-auth-p95-latency (owner: api, metric: P95 response time), nfr-auth-availability (owner: ops, metric: uptime percentage), and nfr-auth-throughput (owner: api, metric: requests per second) as three distinct entries. Each NFR must have a distinct nfr_id; do not bundle multiple quality attributes (e.g., latency + availability) into a single entry — create separate NFR entries so each can be traced, measured, and owned independently.

nfr_id.description: Unique kebab-case identifier for this NFR. Required format (enforced by pattern): nfr-{category}-{condition}. Examples: 'nfr-perf-api-latency', 'nfr-sec-data-encryption', 'nfr-latency-api-response'. Should be stable across spec versions — do not rename after downstream steps reference this ID.

name.description: Human-readable label for this NFR, suitable for dashboards and reports. Example: 'Login API latency', 'Checkout throughput', 'Auth service availability'. Distinct from metric (which names the measured dimension) — name identifies the NFR entry for humans. Optional.

category.description: Quality attribute category for this NFR. Must be one of the 11 canonical values (enforced by enum): latency, throughput, availability, durability, cost, security, privacy, maintainability, usability, portability, energy. Choose the most specific category that matches the requirement. Common mismatches: 'performance' -> use 'latency' or 'throughput'; 'reliability' -> use 'availability' or 'durability'; 'scalability' -> use 'throughput'; 'compliance' -> use 'privacy' or 'security'. Ambiguity decision rule: if a requirement could fit 'security' or 'privacy', use 'security' when the primary concern is access control or encryption, and 'privacy' when the primary concern is PII data handling. Worked examples: 'JWT token must use RS256 signing' -> 'security' (access-control mechanism); 'User email must not appear in application logs' -> 'privacy' (PII data handling). Anti-pattern: using 'security' as a catch-all for all non-functional requirements — requirements about data retention, PII exposure, or consent belong under 'privacy'.

metric.description: Name of the specific measurable dimension this NFR constrains. Must be precise enough to be graphed or queried in a monitoring tool. Format rule: use a noun phrase identifying the signal, not the goal. Vague-to-precise progression examples: 'response time' -> 'P95 HTTP response time for POST /api/orders measured at the load balancer'; 'error rate' -> 'HTTP 5xx error rate as a percentage of total requests per 5-minute window, excluding health checks'; 'memory usage' -> 'peak RSS memory of the auth-service pod under 1000 concurrent sessions'. Further examples: 'uptime percentage', 'mean time to recovery', 'concurrent session count'. Anti-patterns: 'performance' (too vague — which metric?), 'fast response' (adjective, not a metric name), 'SLA' (outcome, not a dimension). Pair with 'unit' so the full measurement is unambiguous: metric='P95 response time' + unit='ms'.

target.description: The measurable threshold this NFR must meet. When using a numeric target, pair with the 'unit' field for context. When using a string target, embed the unit and condition in the string. Examples: 'P95 latency < 200ms under 1000 concurrent users', '99.9% uptime measured monthly', 'AES-256 encryption for all PII fields'. Avoid vague targets like 'fast' or 'secure' — every target should be falsifiable.

oneOf.description: Numeric target value. Use this form only when the target is a raw count or exact value where direction is self-evident from the metric name. Worked examples where numeric form is unambiguous: 99.9 for 'API Uptime Percentage' (higher is better, universally understood), 5 (max retry count — lower is better and obvious from 'max'), 3 (max DB connections per request). If there is any ambiguity about direction, threshold, or operator, use the string form instead. Use string form '< 200ms' not 200 for latency — the operator must be explicit. Anti-pattern: setting target to 200 when you mean 'under 200ms' — without the operator the direction is ambiguous and tooling cannot evaluate compliance.
String target value containing at least one digit. Preferred for expressive thresholds (e.g., '<200ms', '>99.9%', 'P95 < 500ms under 500 VUs').

baseline.description: Current measured value before the optimization target is applied. Provides the pre-improvement reference point, enabling progress tracking. Use a string for measured values with context, or a number for simple numeric baselines. Omit if not yet measured.

oneOf.description: Numeric baseline value before this project begins, in the same units as the target. Use when the baseline is a clean number. Worked example: 450 (current measured P95 latency in ms before optimization — unit is 'ms' so 450 means 450ms). When baseline is unknown, omit the entire baseline field rather than guessing. Never set to 0 unless 0 is the true measured baseline.

Descriptive baseline value when the numeric form is insufficient. Worked examples: '4-6 hours per billing cycle' (current manual reconciliation time before automation); 'unknown' (new system with no prior measurement — do not use 0, which implies a measured value of zero); 'N/A' (new capability with no prior state to measure from — distinct from 'unknown' which implies measurement is possible but not yet done). Include units in the string for ranges: 'P95: 450ms under 500 concurrent users', '< 5% monthly error rate'. Anti-pattern: '0' as a string — use the numeric branch for actual zero measurements; anti-pattern: omitting baseline entirely when current performance is known, as this removes the improvement reference point.

unit.description: Unit of measurement for the metric. Required for numeric targets; include context for string targets when the unit is not embedded. Selection rule: match the unit to your metric and target. If target is '< 200ms', unit is 'ms'. If target is '>= 99.9%', unit is 'percent'. If target is '< 50' (raw count), unit is 'count'. Decision rule: always use the abbreviated canonical form — never the expanded form. Approved abbreviations: 'ms' (milliseconds), 'percent' (percentage points), 'req/s' (requests per second), 'count' (raw integer count), 'MB' (megabytes), 'GB' (gigabytes), 'USD' (currency). Further examples: unit='ms' for a latency NFR, unit='percent' for an availability NFR, unit='req/s' for a throughput NFR, unit='count' for a retry-limit NFR. For custom units not on this list, follow the same abbreviation convention and register the unit in canon/kinds/term.json before use. Anti-patterns: 'milliseconds' (use 'ms'), 'pct' (non-standard abbreviation — use 'percent'), 'percentage' (use 'percent'), 'requests-per-second' (use 'req/s'), leaving unit empty when the target is a numeric value (makes the target dimensionless and unverifiable).

measurement_method.description: How compliance with this NFR is measured. Should specify: the tool or mechanism, the metric collected, and the test conditions. Complete worked examples: 'P95 latency from DataDog APM dashboard — apm.request.duration metric, 5-minute window, production environment only' or 'Weekly reconciliation job exit code from CloudWatch log group /app/reconciliation, filter: EXIT_CODE != 0' or 'Load test with k6: 1000 VUs over 5 minutes, measuring P95 response time at /api/checkout, run in staging before each release'. Should be reproducible by an engineer who hasn't seen this spec. Anti-pattern: 'Measured by monitoring' — does not specify the dashboard, metric name, query, or conditions, making compliance unverifiable.

measurement_frequency.description: How often this metric is measured and evaluated against its target. Decision rules by requirement type: 'real-time' — for latency and availability metrics that must trigger immediate alerts (e.g., P95 API latency, service uptime); 'per-release' — for code quality metrics evaluated at deployment time (e.g., test coverage percentage, lint score); 'monthly' — for cost and business metrics reviewed in billing cycles (e.g., infrastructure spend, monthly active users); 'weekly' — for error rates that need regular review but not real-time alerting (e.g., weekly 5xx error trend). Full enum: 'real-time' (continuous), 'hourly' (aggregated each hour), 'daily' (daily report or alert), 'weekly' (weekly review), 'monthly' (monthly SLA review), 'per-release' (at each deployment), 'on-demand' (manually triggered). Anti-pattern: using 'real-time' for all metrics regardless of cost or actionability — continuous monitoring of low-priority or slowly-changing metrics wastes observability budget and creates alert fatigue. Optional — omit when frequency is determined by the monitoring toolchain.

stage.description: CI/CD pipeline phase through which this NFR is validated. Must be one of: dev, ci, staging, prod (enforced by enum). DISTINCT from environment (where the system runs); stage refers to a CI/CD pipeline phase (where code goes THROUGH). Common mismatches: 'mvp' -> use 'dev'; 'ga' -> use 'prod'.

owner.description: Team or role accountable for meeting and monitoring this NFR. Must be one of 8 canonical values: 'api' (backend services), 'ui' (frontend/UX), 'system' (platform/infrastructure), 'ops' (operations/DevOps), 'data' (data engineering/analytics), 'product', 'business', 'engineering'. Decision rule: choose the team that controls the code path most responsible for this NFR. For latency NFRs on API endpoints: 'api'. For availability/uptime NFRs: 'ops'. For data retention NFRs: 'data'.

trace.description: Traceability links connecting this NFR to the upstream charter success metrics or capabilities it quantifies. Every NFR must trace to at least one upstream success metric or capability using type='derives_from'. Complete worked example for an auth latency NFR: [{"type": "derives_from", "id": "metric-auth-p95-latency", "note": "Charter success metric directly motivating this NFR"}, {"type": "constrains", "id": "cap-user-authentication", "note": "This latency budget applies to the authentication capability"}]. The derives_from entry is required; the constrains entry is optional but recommended when the NFR applies to a specific capability. Secondary traces using type='constrains' are allowed for capabilities that must operate within this NFR's limits (e.g., a cap-* ID from spec/01_capabilities.json), but they do not substitute for a derives_from link to a metric-* or cap-* charter source. Minimum: one trace per NFR. NFRs without at least one derives_from trace link cannot be validated against charter commitments and will fail canonical-integrity and traceability-check.

items.description: A traceability reference linking this NFR to the upstream charter success metric or capability it quantifies. At step 07, use type 'derives_from' pointing to a metric-* ID from spec/00_charter.json success_metrics or a cap-* ID from spec/01_capabilities.json. Example: {"type": "derives_from", "id": "metric-checkout-latency", "note": "NFR quantifies the checkout page load time success metric"}. Secondary traces to FR or API IDs (type 'constrains') are allowed but do not substitute for a charter or capability link. NFRs without a derives_from trace to metric-* or cap-* cannot be validated against charter success criteria and will fail canonical-integrity checks.

metric_ref.description: Canonical reference binding the 'metric' string to a shared vocabulary entry in the canonical registry. Format rule: use a canonicalRef object with id, kind, and optional label. The id must use the cn: URN scheme. Example: {"id": "cn:core:metric:p95-response-time", "kind": "metric", "label": "P95 Response Time"}. Decision guidance: look up available metric IDs with 'specdev canonical-lint canon --repo-root ./devspec_toolkit' before authoring. Anti-patterns: omitting metric_ref and relying on a free-form metric string (breaks canonical-integrity checks); using a bare string instead of a canonicalRef object; inventing new metric IDs without adding them to the canon registry first.

unit_ref.description: Canonical reference binding the 'unit' string to a normalised unit entry in the canonical registry. Kind is structurally pinned to 'unit'. Always pair with the 'unit' field. Worked examples: if unit is 'ms', use {"id": "cn:core:unit:ms", "kind": "unit"}; if unit is 'percent', use {"id": "cn:core:unit:percent", "kind": "unit"}; if unit is 'count', use {"id": "cn:core:unit:count", "kind": "unit"}. Decision guidance: always use the canonical abbreviated form (ms, percent, count) as the id suffix. Anti-patterns: omitting unit_ref when unit is present (breaks canonical-integrity checks).

stage_ref.description: Canonical reference binding the 'stage' enum value to its entry in the canonical stage registry. Format rule: use a canonicalRef object with kind 'stage' and a cn: URN id matching the stage value. Worked example: if stage is 'production', use {"id": "cn:core:stage:production", "kind": "stage", "label": "production"}; if stage is 'ci', use {"id": "cn:core:stage:ci", "kind": "stage", "label": "CI"}. Decision guidance: stage_ref must agree with the 'stage' string — mismatches are flagged by canonical-lint. Anti-patterns: using a stage_ref id that differs from the 'stage' field value (e.g., stage='production' but stage_ref id='cn:core:stage:staging' — causes canonical-integrity lint failure); omitting stage_ref while providing stage (partial canonical coverage leaves the entry unverifiable).

environment_ref.description: Canonical reference to the environment where this NFR is measured. Decision rule: include environment_ref only when the NFR target differs by environment. Worked example: a latency target of 200ms in production but 500ms in staging requires two separate NFR entries — one with environment_ref {"id": "cn:core:environment:production", "kind": "environment", "label": "production"} and target '< 200ms', and another with environment_ref {"id": "cn:core:environment:staging", "kind": "environment", "label": "staging"} and target '< 500ms'. Counter-example: a code coverage requirement of >= 80% applies identically in all environments — omit environment_ref entirely. Do NOT use bare environment names — this field requires a full canonicalRef object with id and kind (label recommended). Anti-pattern: including environment_ref set to a value meaning 'all environments' — if the target is the same everywhere, omit the field entirely.
